title: Porridge with Apple and Cinnamon
subtitle: Creamy oat porridge with grated apple and warming spice
excerpt: Grated apple stirred into porridge as it cooks disappears into the oats, sweetening them gently and adding body. Cinnamon and a drizzle of honey make it taste like breakfast should in October.
sourceNotes: Apple and cinnamon porridge is a widely made British autumn and winter breakfast. The technique of cooking grated apple directly into the oats, rather than serving it on top, distributes the flavour evenly and requires no separate preparation.

content.text: Apple and cinnamon porridge is one of the best things about the mornings getting darker. Grating the apple directly into the pan means it cooks into the oats and becomes part of the porridge rather than a separate topping, the sweetness spreads all the way through and the oats thicken around it. It takes eight minutes and produces a bowl of porridge that warms you through rather than just filling.
Grate the apple, skin on, directly into the pan. Add the oats, milk, and a pinch of salt. Stir to combine.
Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring regularly. Reduce to low and cook for 5 to 6 minutes until thick and creamy.
Stir in the cinnamon in the final minute. Spoon into warm bowls and drizzle with honey to serve.

Use a coarse grater and grate the {{apple-eating}} apple, skin on, directly over the saucepan before anything else goes in, so the juice goes in too. Core the apple first and stop grating when you reach the core. The skin adds a little colour and texture and does not need removing. Cox, Braeburn, or any firm eating apple works well; avoid very watery varieties that will make the porridge loose.

Add the {{porridge-oats}} porridge oats to the pan with the grated apple. Pour in the {{whole-milk}} whole milk and add a pinch of {{sea-salt-flakes}} sea salt flakes, salt is not optional in porridge; it lifts the flavour significantly. Stir everything together and place over a medium heat. Bring slowly to a gentle simmer, stirring regularly with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula. Once it begins to bubble, reduce the heat to low and cook for five to six minutes, stirring often, until the oats have absorbed the milk and the porridge is thick and creamy. Stir in the {{cinnamon-ground}} ground cinnamon in the last minute of cooking.

Porridge made with all milk is richer and creamier than porridge made with water or a mix. For a lighter result, use half milk and half water, the texture is less thick but still pleasant. Pure water gives a plainer, more austere result that suits people who find all-milk porridge too heavy. This recipe uses all milk, which suits the apple and cinnamon well.

Spoon into warm bowls and drizzle over the {{honey}} honey. The honey should go on at the table rather than in the pan, cooking it in reduces its flavour and loses the contrast of a fresh, sweet drizzle against the warm, spiced oats. A splash of cold milk around the edge of the bowl is the traditional Scottish approach and cools the porridge enough to start eating immediately. A few thin slices of raw apple on top adds a pleasant crunch if you prefer something to eat against the soft oats.

Apple and cinnamon porridge is an autumn and winter breakfast. It makes most sense from September through to March when the mornings are cold and a bowl of something warm and sweet actually earns its place. It is quick enough for a weekday, the whole thing, including grating, takes ten minutes from standing at the hob to bowl on the table.

Porridge is sticking to the bottom of the pan: the heat is too high or the stirring has been too infrequent. Porridge needs regular attention, stir every thirty seconds or so once it starts to thicken, and use a medium-low rather than medium heat.

Porridge is too thick: add a splash more milk and stir it in over the heat for another minute. Porridge thickens as it stands, so if it looks right in the pan it will be firmer in the bowl, cook it slightly looser than you want it.
Apple flavour is not coming through: the apple may have been quite mild. Stir in a small extra pinch of cinnamon and taste again, cinnamon amplifies the apple note considerably.
